analysis.one_liner: Requires TV drug ads to show the drug's list price for a typical 30-day supply.
analysis.headline: The bill has received no action since its July 2025 introduction and sits without a hearing or vote in two House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to write a rule requiring TV ads for prescription drugs covered by Medicare or Medicaid to print the drug's list price — what a typical 30-day supply costs at full list — on screen. The idea is that consumers seeing a drug ad would know up front whether the drug costs hundreds or thousands of dollars. The rule would take effect within a year of the bill becoming law, and regulators would decide whether to extend the requirement to other kinds of ads [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and consumers who see prescription drug ads on television would see the drug's list price for a typical 30-day regimen printed on screen, letting them compare prices before asking a doctor for a drug [S2] [S3]. Because the rule covers drugs paid for under Medicare or Medicaid, it reaches the most expensive widely advertised drugs [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Direct-to-consumer TV ads for Medicare- and Medicaid-covered drugs would have to include a truthful, on-screen statement of the drug's list price for a typical 30-day regimen or course of treatment
The price shown must be current as of the first day of the quarter the ad airs, so the figure would track list-price changes rather than going stale
Regulators would also decide whether to extend disclosure to other advertising formats, set the exact format, and choose enforcement mechanisms, which could broaden the requirement beyond television

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers whose drugs are covered by Medicare or Medicaid would bear the cost of displaying list prices in their TV ads, and broadcasters and streaming services could see reduced drug-ad spending if disclosure dampens demand for high-priced drugs [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and TV ad revenue

drawbacks.text: The required figure is the drug's list price, which is usually far higher than what insured patients, Medicare, or Medicaid actually pay after discounts and negotiated rates — so the number on screen could confuse more than inform

The bill leaves the hard choices to regulators: it does not itself decide whether the rule covers internet or radio ads, how the price must be displayed, or how violations are enforced, all of which would be settled in a rulemaking that could be delayed or softened
A list-price disclosure could push some drug makers to cut TV advertising, which reduces the information (as well as the demand-building) that ads provide to viewers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real but modest: seeing a list price in an ad gives viewers useful context, though it is not the price most people actually pay after insurance. The main costs fall on drug makers and on TV outlets that sell their ads, and the bill's biggest weakness is that it delegates almost every design and enforcement decision to a future rulemaking, so its practical effect depends on how a rule gets written. It is a transparency measure, not a price control — it informs consumers rather than lowering any price.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and sent to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing or vote ever since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 22, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee
No further action — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history, and Congress is still in session
The bill's cosponsors include three Republicans and one Democrat, giving it support from both parties

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened yet, no one is better off than before. The status quo — drug ads with no required price disclosure — remains in place while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers are worse off; drug makers unchanged

for.name: Reps. Don Bacon, Angie Craig, and Bryan Steil
for.role: Original cosponsors (Bacon of Nebraska, Steil of Wisconsin; Craig of Minnesota)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it Republican as well as Democratic support

sides.party_line_note: The bill is sponsored by a Democrat with a mixed-party team of cosponsors — three Republicans and one Democrat — and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill requires drug ads to display the list price of a typical 30-day regimen for Medicare- or Medicaid-covered drugs, a disclosure the industry has generally resisted because showing high prices on screen can suppress demand. Consumers gain price visibility; manufacturers lose a measure of persuasive control over their ads.

industries.industry: Broadcast, cable, and streaming TV ad sellers
industries.note: Pharmaceutical advertising is one of the largest revenue sources for broadcast, cable, and streaming television. If disclosure makes drug ads less effective and companies buy fewer of them, these companies could lose ad revenue while consumers gain information.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has a bipartisan sponsor team but has had no action since its July 2025 referral to two committees. The most likely path, as with most House bills, is that it stays in committee and never reaches a floor vote unless its sponsors attach it to a larger health or drug-pricing package.
